title: The night of the firstborn (Exodus 11–12)
hookLine: blood on the doorposts, and the Lord passes over the houses
tomorrow: bread with no time to rise

lines: THE WHOLE EVENING IS THE ANSWER.
cards: Every spring, at a table full of family, the youngest child who can read stands up, sometimes nervous, sometimes showing off, and sings a question. Ma nishtanah halailah hazeh mikol haleilot?
Why is this night different from all other nights? Why the flat bread? Why the bitter herbs?
Why do we dip, and lean? The whole long evening that follows is the answer. It's called the seder, and it retells one night.

teach.h: A LAMB, BLOOD ON THE DOORPOSTS.
teach.b: Moses warns Pharaoh of one final blow: at midnight, every firstborn in Egypt will die. Then God gives the Israelites very specific instructions. Each household takes a lamb.
On the fourteenth day of the month, they slaughter it, and with a bunch of hyssop put some of its blood on the two doorposts and the top of the door.
They roast it and eat it that night, with flat bread and bitter herbs, dressed for travel, shoes on, staff in hand, in a hurry. No one is to go out of the house until morning.
God says: "when I see the blood, I will pass over you."
That's Pesach, from a Hebrew root that means to pass over, or, some say, to hover over, protecting. At midnight it happens.
There's a great cry in Egypt, the text says, for there was not a house where there was not one dead. It's a terrible night.
The Torah doesn't hide it, and Jewish tradition doesn't treat it as simple; the spilled wine and the silenced angels come later this week.
And before anyone has even left, God tells them to make this night a memorial forever. The Torah says your children will ask: "What mean ye by this service?"

teach.h: AND THOU SHALT TELL THY SON.
teach.b: And the commandment is: "And thou shalt tell thy son in that day."
That's why a child asks the questions at the seder. Freedom isn't only something that happened. It's something you tell, out loud, to the next person, every year.

how: Every spring Jews hold a Passover seder at home, retelling the Exodus from the Haggadah; a child asks why this night is different, and the family eats matzah and bitter herbs and tells the story in answer.

o: a lamp: a light left burning until dawn
a wedding: a feast for a bride and groom
Passover: to pass over, or hover over and protect

games.q: what's inside the night — tap the pairs.
p: the whole evening is the answer

s: the Israelites were told to watch from outside
no one was to go out of the door of his house until morning.
the command to retell it came before they even left Egypt
the instructions for remembering are given on the night itself.
Jewish tradition treats the death of the firstborn as simple and joyful
the Torah calls it a great cry, and the tradition remembers the cost.

games.q: you're in a house in Goshen. the blood is on the doorposts, the lamb is roasting, and it's nearly midnight. what does the text tell you to do?
o: go out and see what happens.
stay inside, dressed to leave, and eat.
games.why: stay in, shoes on, staff in hand, eat in haste. no one goes out until morning. the next day, they leave.

practice: If you have something small nearby, a piece of bread, a cracker, some fruit, hold it a moment before you eat; if not, just imagine it.
Think of something you were brought out of: a hard time, a narrow place, something that once held you. Then eat it slowly, and let it be a small memorial.

wordCard.voice: Pesach. Passover. The night God passed over the marked houses, and the name of the holiday that retells it every spring.

orig.note: Hebrew: Passover. from p-s-ch, to pass over, or to hover over and protect.

carryVoice: Your line: this night is different. The answer always starts with a child's question. Until tomorrow.
